time.desc: Citing the conclusion of a national security review, the government of an allied country ordered the short video platform to cease operations and close local offices, but did not prohibit the public from continuing to use the app.

A federal appeals court in a certain country upheld the legislative requirement of “divest or ban”, confirming that the ownership of the platform’s parent company poses a national security risk and setting a divestment cutoff.
The platform submitted an urgent request to the Supreme Court, seeking to suspend the implementation of the "stripping or banning" arrangement until the final hearing.
The Supreme Court quickly accepted the platform's appeal against the relevant legislation and scheduled oral arguments, but did not immediately issue a temporary blocking order.
The incoming national leader files papers with the Supreme Court, asking for a delay in the implementation of the key "divest or ban" cutoff to allow the new government to seek a political solution
The country's judiciary filed papers with the Supreme Court opposing the postponement request, highlighting the serious national security risks posed by the platform's foreign control

The Supreme Court held oral arguments on whether the platform should be forced to divest or face a ban, with questions from the justices showing an overall greater focus on national security arguments.

For the first time, a full Court of Appeal panel has unambiguously determined that ownership of Platform X's parent company poses a substantiated national security threat, and the head of the judiciary publicly applauded the ruling.
Platform X filed an emergency injunction application with the Court of Appeal requesting a stay of execution, and the judiciary filed an objection on the same day
Platform X Allied subsidiary files emergency motion in local federal court seeking judicial review of order closing local operations
Parent company appeals to court seeking extension of divestment or injunction cutoff until after incoming leader takes office

The Federal Court of Appeal once again rejected Platform X’s request to suspend the execution of the injunction. The platform announced that it would appeal to the highest judicial authority and announced that it may shut down by the cutoff.
Several civil rights and free speech organizations jointly submitted an amicus brief to the highest judicial body urging to prevent the ban from taking effect.

Platform X An Region N subsidiary of an allied country filed an emergency motion with a local federal court seeking judicial review of a government order requiring it to close local operations, requesting that it be vacated or returned to the government for review.
Federal appeals court again rejects Platform X's request for a stay of injunction, refusing to halt "stripping or disabling" law until case is filed Court D, Platform X says it will appeal to Court D
Two senior Institution F MPs have written to Comparison Company A and Comparison Company B asking the companies to remove Platform X from their app stores before a legal cutoff

Designate Leader A made his first public statement at a rally in support of Platform X continuing to operate in Country A, and later met with Platform X CEO C EO_C, a reversal from his earlier push for a ban

Platform X first invoked the freedom of speech clause of Law F to defend Court D, pointing out that the legislation does not prohibit Company O, Company P and other applications belonging to Country B, indicating that it targets its social media content rather than data security

As the risk of a ban approaches, Platform X creator groups are anxious because of the disruption to their income from live broadcasts and reward programs. Some people have begun to turn their energy to platforms such as competing social graphics applications and comparison video platforms.
